I started using Authy long ago because it supports multiple devices and isn't linked to any other account (Google/Microsoft).
If you use Authy, turn off 'allow multi-device' and SIM-swapping isn't an issue.
Authy makes it hard to migrate away. Anyone know how to get the seed of the 2FA codes? Is there really no export option?
I just migrated off of Authy last week... Never liked it but they make it extremely difficult to export your data. Twilio really doesn't want you to export your data for 'security' reasons.
Twilio confirms data breach: hackers leak 33M Authy user phone numbers via an unauthenticated endpoint.
This doesn't scare me because in Authy you also set a password which without you cannot access the codes. The phone number here just acts as a username.
When I tried SendGrid it was super annoying that I had to install yet another Authenticator app on my phone (Authy). It's bizarre Twilio decided to get into the Authenticator business at all.
I found an information exposure vuln on the Authy user registration endpoint... It took them two years to fix it.
That app is so dumb. Completely negated the usefulness of TOTP. Needs just to die already.

They intentionally make it really hard to migrate your data off their app under the premise of 'security'. Now they are EOL'ing desktop apps, which are extremely convenient to use, despite the terrible UX.

My guess is that most of the people who worked on Authy have fallen by the wayside after the Twilio acquisition. It's annoying every time I have to search the boxes: can't we please have alphabetization?
I use Authy with Face ID protecting the entire app on my phone... they'd still need the 2FA codes from my phone [even if password manager compromised].
After a lot of trouble, I was able to extract my private keys from Authy by installing their deprecated Chrome extension and using some hacky javascript found in a gist.
Note how insane the Authy export instructions are: 'Paste in a bunch of code to an Electron app running Authy in debug mode to dump the tokens as QR codes.' It works but :yikes:
The Twilio exploit allowed the hackers to add a new device to existing Authy accounts. This allowed them to sync the keys between devices within the same account.
services with Authy-integrated MFA (like Twitch) are 'managed' by Authy so it can regenerate the secret on the fly; your previously extracted secret will no longer be valid.
I feel like this misses the problem with Authy. There are hundreds of 2FA alternatives, but when my 401K provider requires Authy specifically with no generic 2FA option, THAT is the problem.
I will also never forgive Authy for removing desktop support with near immediate deprecation and no way to export off their platform. I will never use another Twilio product again after that.
I've been using Authy as a backup for 1Password's 2FA since in a worst-case scenario I can get a replacement SIM card and get back into my 1Password account via recovery. Authy is fine for this use.
Tangentially: I just got rid of Authy, it took me 2h to migrate everything, moved to apple passwords.

User migrated off Authy the week before the breach, saying they never liked it and it is extremely difficult to export data. They used the alexzorin/authy GitHub project, then learned it relied on the same unauthenticated endpoint used in the breach.

User reports finding an information exposure vulnerability on Authy's registration endpoint. Given an Authy user's phone number, it returned their other numbers, devices, timestamps and email addresses. They say it took Twilio two years to fix.
User calls Authy 'basically unsupported' and says they moved their accounts to 1Password when the macOS app's end of life was announced.

Alternatives suggested for leaving Authy: Authenticator Pro with encrypted backups, or Aegis. Because Authy lacks easy export, one user suggests moving a few entries at a time and running both authenticators side by side.

Authy intentionally makes migrating data off the app hard under the premise of 'security'. Exporting requires fairly deep technical knowledge and a specific desktop app version, which is now being EOL'd. The user stopped using Authy for these reasons.

On Apple silicon Macs, users can still install the Authy iOS/iPad app from the App Store as a desktop stop-gap. It works but isn't first-class; swipe-to-delete requires enabling alternative touch settings.

User says the Authy desktop app always sucked but was more convenient than reaching for the phone. TOTP codes often got out of sync until they backed out of an app's section and waited for the code to flip.
User who uses Authy almost daily finds it very convenient. They don't always have their phone nearby, and the desktop app has more than once prevented them being locked out of a service.
After a lot of trouble, user extracted their private keys from Authy by installing the deprecated Chrome extension and running hacky JavaScript from a gist.

Long-time Authy user (6–7 years) exported keys via the deprecated Chrome extension as a page of QR codes, printed it as backup, and moved 20+ accounts to Raivo in about 5 minutes. They had grown uncomfortable with Authy being tied to their phone number.

User lost access to their Twitch account after Twitch moved its 2FA to Authy. Their Authy account, tied to a phone number, had been handed to a former coworker for SendGrid access, and neither Twitch nor Authy support would help. They switched to Bitwarden for 2FA.
User says the real problem with Authy is lock-in by services: their 401K provider requires Authy to log in and offers no generic 2FA option.
User says they will never forgive Authy for removing desktop support with near-immediate deprecation and no way to export off the platform, and will never use another Twilio product.

User keeps Authy as a backup for their 1Password 2FA because, being tied to their phone number, a replacement SIM restores access. This was tested when their phone was pickpocketed in Amsterdam. They find Authy fine for this use.
User spent about 2 hours migrating everything off Authy to Apple Passwords, which has a solid export feature. They will never forgive Authy/Twilio for deliberately making exports impossible.

User calls Authy one of the worst-designed iOS apps they've used: a scrolling icon list and 10pt service names make finding codes tedious with more than ~3 services. They like the encrypted backup but dislike the service lock-in.
User likes Authy, saying they've barely noticed it exists and are glad to use one app for most of their 2FA services.
User lost access to all their tokens after upgrading phones, having assumed codes would port automatically because the app was linked to their number. They say they'll never use Authy again.
User uses Authy for all their 2FA accounts and calls it awesome. They describe Google's app as crap and Authy's app as sexy and fast.
User failed to set up Authy's Bluetooth desktop sync on OS X 10.8 with an iPhone 4S on iOS 7. The desktop app showed an empty device list despite granting Bluetooth access.
